name: Illusory Correlation
description: People perceive a meaningful relationship between two traits, groups, or events because the pairing feels salient or memorable, not because a real correlation exists. Distinctive co-occurrences can look diagnostic even when they are just noise.
design_relevance_note: Relevant to how teams interpret dashboards, anecdotes, persona traits, or user-segment stories: a vivid pairing (for example, one memorable user type plus one memorable failure mode) can be mistaken for a real causal or correlational pattern.
prevalence_note: Well known in social psychology, stereotype research, and data-interpretation contexts, but not a mainstream named heuristic in routine product-design discourse.

findings.description: Classic experimental social-perception evidence showed that observers can over-infer a relationship between group membership and behavior from distinctive pairings, even when the underlying data do not warrant that association. This is the core illusory-correlation pattern: salient co-occurrence gets mistaken for real correlation.
findings.source_title: Illusory correlation in interpersonal perception: A cognitive basis of stereotypic judgments

findings.description: Reported to show that clinicians and lay judges perceived correlations between Rorschach response themes and clinical diagnoses that did not actually exist in the underlying data, driven by pre-existing semantic/verbal associations rather than genuine diagnostic validity -- the foundational demonstration of illusory correlation, independently confirming and predating the corpus's existing Hamilton & Gifford (1976) evidence. This description is drawn from the paper's well-established secondary characterization, not independently verified against the primary text this session (see the source's own verification_note).
findings.source_title: Illusory correlation as an obstacle to the use of valid psychodiagnostic signs.
